PHIL STEELE PUBLICATIONS 25935 Detroit Road Ste. 183 • Cleveland, OH 44145 1-866-918-7711 • PhilSteele.com PHIL ON TWITTER @PHILSTEELE042 Conference Coordinators: Phil Steele PUBLISHER / EDITOR Rich Cirminiello.....Big12/MW/Sun Belt Dan Gilles...................Big Ten/PAC-12 Adam Jones.................................AAC Jim Seman..............Independent/MAC Chris Van Dine..ACC/CUSA/SEC/Media Welcome to my 2026 College Football Preview. This is the 32nd edition and this is the biggest and BEST ever that I have produced. The main reason for that is the transfer portal or should I say the lack of a second transfer portal window! Last year was very frustrating for me as we had some unfortunate typos with all the scrambling we did with the 2nd portal closing April 27. This year I did not have to redo 138 team pages in May as it was like old times with the rosters being mostly set after spring. I am very pleased to report that this year I set a record talking to coaches from 133 of the 138 schools! The calls take on average about an hour apiece as we go over the entire roster and I get thoughts on the individual players and each position. This accounts for the high level of accuracy I have in the three and four deep PSL's that I list on the pages. I feel the pages are in the best shape they have ever been in due to that factor and it tops my record of 125 I set last year! These calls all take place post spring after they have had their exit interviews with the players. It is the eight straight year we have set a record. I would like to thank each and every one of the coaches who took some of their valuable time to go over my team pages with me! As a side note sometimes I make my own changes to the three deep based on a projection so if it differs from the coaches three deep that is my fault not theirs as it is the Phil Steele magazine. A common theme talking to the coaches this year is almost every single coach felt that they were more or a team in the spring and that they could coach the players harder. They did not have to worry about players leaving after spring was over and the players did not have to worry that the coach was going to replace them after the spring with a new portal addition. I believe this will result in improved play on the ﬁeld this year. Please keep it to one portal window and have it pre spring in the future. Learﬁeld has taken over the printing and distribution of the magazine which has taken some weight off my shoulders. They also provide a topnotch digital app. If you get the digital version of the magazine you will notice that we update it in June, July, August and even into September with any Associates & Contributors Tierra Clarke Charlie Fadel Todd Gebhardt Rosemary Hammons Dennis Macklin Mike Perry Anne Pilawski Gena Robbins Savannah Steele Jon Van Dine Edwin Vereen Ken Willinger changes that happen in those months. Getting both versions of the magazine is your best bet, so check out the page to your left. The magazine has come a long way from the 1995 black and white ﬁrst edition that had 192 total pages and covered just 86 FBS teams. As I type this, the other magazines are already on the shelves which means they had to go to press way late April/ early May before many teams springs were even over! I am very proud to not only be a Heisman voter but also either a voter or committee member of 21 different awards. That is a great honor, so I invest a lot of time and effort into each award and committee that I am on. I list them in the back of the magazine. I would also like to thank my staff who toiled away for seven months and the last few weeks were putting in 20-40 hours of OT per week to get this magazine not only out, but making sure it was accurate. This is far from a one man job and we would not have made it without their hard work over seven months. I could not do this project without their care and effort. I plan on doing this magazine til at least Volume 50! We poured seven months of effort into producing this magazine and ﬁnally.....I would like to thank YOU for purchasing it! FOOTBALL DAYS A YEAR 5 36 By Phil Steele Pictured to the left is the set up I have at my ofﬁce with 12 TV's to take in all the action on a Saturday. The photos (taken 11/29/25) is the actual setup at my ofﬁce. At my home ofﬁce I only have eight TV’s in front of my desk but they are all big screens. Many people ask me, “How can you watch 12 games at once?” When we took the pictures, we were able to get action on all the TV's at one time. We took numerous pictures and Todd pasted them in to capture this. Keep in mind the average play takes four to six seconds then there is down time. I usually focus on the 4 TV’s directly in front of my desk (lower right hand corner) and watch every play of those then in the ring of 5 TV's around those four, I capture every other play. The ﬁnal section (I call them TV's #10, #11 and #12) I capture about every 3rd play. One of these days we will have to hold a drawing of some sort and let a long-time reader come in and get this experience! Now I will provide you some key notes for you to use the magazine and perhaps even the website to the fullest. First of all, I would like to thank Krifka at Barnes & Noble for basically saving the magazine. During the Covid year, I was on the verge of hanging it up as I did not know if they were going to play football and I invest way too much time and money into getting the magazine produced each year. My staff and I put in a legitimate 6.5 months of labor into the magazine and I work year round on football averaging 102 hours a week during football and another 75-80 hours a week during magazine season. My "free months" are during the end of June, all of July and the start of August. Just when I announced on Twitter that we would NOT be on the newsstands in 2020, Krifka at Barnes & Noble called me and said they NEEDED the magazine and purchased them from us direct. She took a BIG risk as it was not really known if they would be playing football at all in 2020! We did distribute in 2020 thanks to that risk that Krifka took and now I am no longer thinking of folding but instead looking ahead to producing this labor of love another 30 years. In 2023 Krifka came up with the idea that we could put two different covers into the same store!!! We jumped at the opportunity and if you are reading this in your local Barnes & Noble you probably have a choice of covers. Great Idea Krifka! Tracy, who is my daily contact at B&N, does a tremendous job and she is a great pleasure to work with! A big thanks to Barnes & Noble!!! As far as some speciﬁcs. On each conference page I list unit rankings. One area that may raise some questions is the coaches' ranking. I take into account years at the program, as it is usually a two to three-year process for new head coaches to get up to 100% speed at their new school. I have most ﬁrst-year HC’s ranked lower than you would normally think due to this process and then bring them up in the rankings the next two years. In their 3rd year well over half the teams consist of their own players and recruits and that is when I rank them completely according to their coaching productivity. This year's ﬁrst year head coaches are rated lower than they normally would be. The top player rankings in the front of the magazine are a pure NFL ranking. If you look at my All-American Teams you will ﬁnd WR Jeremiah Smith on my AllAmerican Team. However, you will not ﬁnd him on my Draft Eligible Players List in the front because he is a true Sophomore and he is NOT eligible for the 2025 NFL Draft. You will also notice that sometimes I have a player rated 1st Team All-Conference and yet in the front of the magazine, he is listed behind a player who I list 2nd Team. My All-Conference lists are how I think the players will perform this year in college football. The lists in the front are where we think they are in terms of NFL Draft possibilities. Those lists are prepared by Josh Buchanan from DraftScout.com who does a great job. 2

I would also like to thank the head coaches who talked to me this year. Each year the number gets bigger. This year the number rose 125+ coaches! There were six complete conferences where I talked to the coach from every team in the conference! We go over every player on their roster and they put my two-deeps in the right order and tell me a little something about every player that will contribute this year. These calls generally take about an hour each. These calls are off the record and most coaches give me the legitimate story on the players. I do want to point out that this is the Phil Steele magazine and it has my name on the front. Sometimes even if a coach tells me to list ‘player A’ first and ‘player B’ second, I may do the opposite as I like to project starters into the season rather than out of spring. One big change brought on by the Transfer Portal is how I grade returning starters. Now if a full-time starter for one team has transferred to another and is listed as a starter out of the spring, I will include them as a returning starter! My old rule was if 5 starters were lost there could not have more than 6 returning, but the portal is changing the way many things are done!!! Finally this is year 32 for the magazine and people wonder when I am going to retire. I have a date. I will retire after issue 50 in 2044 so look forward to doing this for 2 more decades (God willing!). In the early days of the magazine the point size got down to as small as 6 or 7 point text and almost every sentence was heavily abbreviated. When I was hired full-time by ESPN in 2017 (for three years) they did not allow me to use any abbreviations, which greatly changed my writing style. Now I still try to cram as much information into the magazine as possible so there are still abbreviations in the text, but you should have noticed there are a lot fewer than 10 years ago. There is one section of the magazine that is full blown Old School Phil Steele and that is the 2025 Recap Section! If you are an English Major and hung up on grammar, full spelling of words and complete sentences, then DO NOT read the 2025 recaps. I watch every game on Saturday then go through the play-by-play of each game and write my recaps. My quick history after 12 games combined is generally about a column and half of text as I want you to know the ebbs and flows of each game and when the turning points and important things happened. In the chop down process I am turning to complete abbreviations. The first thing I did was take out all of the following words; left, at, by, went, had, in, the, to, for, and, then, got, and among others. Check out the abbreviations on page 3. The postal service has a two letter abbreviation for each state including ones like Massachusetts and Connecticut. When I refer to the school names you will notice heavy use of two letter abbreviations. I do not include the “U” for University. There is a glaring lack of “U’s” in this text as almost all were taken out. If you are on the Mississippi St page then they are abbreviated MS. This is a college football preview magazine and all the schools in here are Colleges or Universities. I am a substance over style 3

#1 MOST ACCURATE OVER 31 YEARS! By Aaron Taylor Aaron Taylor is the founder of the Joe Moore Award, the only honor in college football that annually recognizes the most outstanding offensive line unit — a reﬂection of his lifelong commitment to the trenches. A consensus All-American and Lombardi Award winner at Notre Dame, Taylor went on to play six seasons in the NFL, where he was a key part of the Green Bay Packers' Super Bowl XXXI championship team. Now a lead college football analyst for CBS Sports, Taylor has become a tireless advocate for offensive line play, helping elevate the visibility and value of the position through the Joe Moore Award, which stands as one of the most respected and distinctive honors in all of football Teamwork. It’s what makes football the greatest game on the planet — and nowhere is that more obvious than along the line of scrimmage. The offensive line is the one spot on the ﬁeld where individual achievement only matters if the whole group is clicking. The O-line is football in its purest form: ﬁve guys with a common goal, doing the dirty work so others can shine. That’s the kind of football I grew up on. It’s the kind Coach Joe Moore demanded. And it’s the kind Phil Steele has been telling better than anyone for over 30 years. See, when you cover college football for a living like I have for the past couple decades, you learn quickly that you’re only as good as the information you use to educate, entertain, or spark some debate. Opinions come and go, but facts? Those get you hired or ﬁred. And with 138 teams, the chaos of NIL, and the transfer portal spinning faster than I am these days, nobody keeps it straighter than Phil Steele. His preview is the go-to for those of us who have to know — not guess — about the who’s who and what’s what of college football. His accuracy has stood the test of time...and trust me, neither of us would still be doing this if it hadn’t! About six years ago, I brought Phil onto the voting committee for the Joe Moore Award — the only award in college football that honors a group instead of an individual. Now, don’t get me wrong — the only thing offensive about Phil’s “line” is his stat line. At 5'11", 210, he’s built more for spreadsheets than scoop blocks. But what he brings to the table is unmatched in the publishing game: knowledge of the game, and relationships across the country to back it up. When you know every coach in America and can cut through the clutter like Phil can, you bring a perspective that’s not just unique — it’s essential. He serves as a built-in check and balance for the rest of us meatheads grinding through tape who either played or coached the position. Phil’s Here is an example from this past season, so you see exactly how the scoring is done. Let’s take a look at the SEC. And honestly, that kind of steady, reliable contribution is exactly what the Joe Moore Award has come to represent. Given that nothing like this had ever been done before, it’s hard to believe we just hit our 10-year anniversary. What started as a simple way to honor the men who move other men against their will, has grown into the fastest-growing award in college football. Along the way, we’ve partnered with DonJoy®, thanks to our friends at Enovis Corporation, who have been the perfect partner from Day 1 and just re-signed to help us keep it rolling. They understand better than most that trench life isn’t pretty — but reliability and safety aren’t optional when you’re living in the middle of it. And after a decade of honoring the toughest units in the country, this past season delivered one of the proudest and most meaningful moments in the award’s history. Army — yes, a service academy — broke through and took home the biggest trophy in all of sports. First time ever for a service academy or a Group of 5 team. How did they do it? The old-fashioned way: toughness, consistency, effort, and ﬁnish. Every snap. 6

I am very proud to be one of two non Offensive Lineman or OL coach that is on the Joe Moore committee. I am amazed how much ﬁlm these guys watch and break down and how OL technical the calls get. I guarantee you there is not an award committee that watches as much ﬁlm as these guys do. They care deeply about the award. All of us contribute to narrowing down the list to the midseason group and then their magic begins. I have to be honest when we do the conference call to establish the ﬁnalists, I mostly sit back and listen to Aaron Taylor, Cole Cubelic, Duke Manyweather, Geoff Schwarz, Mike Golic Jr, Lance Zierlein, Brandon Thorn, Randy Cross, Charles Arbuckle, Harry Hiestand, Greg Hudson and Steve Shankweiler talk about what they learned watching each of the semiﬁnalists complete games. Stassen.com - Chris Stassen started the website breaking down preseason magazines back in 1993 before my magazine was even started. In the ﬁrst two years of my mag (‘94’95) I predicted teams in the order of overall record not conference record and it cost me. I also did not forecast every league and was hit with penalties. The ﬁrst year I ﬁnished #13 of 16 magazines and in 1996, I was #19 of 21. I discovered his site in 1997 and started forecasting conference based on conference order and ﬁnished near the top almost every year since. Adding points up and even including 1995 and 1996 I have the most accurate mag over 31 years combined. If you look at page 6 it has a sample of how the scoring works. Pick a team ﬁrst and they ﬁnish 5th and you get 4 points. Pick a team ﬁrst and they ﬁnish ﬁrst 0 points. Like golf LOW score wins. There is no personal bias, strictly Math and that is how the scores are accumalated. Every Saturday. No excuses. No ﬂash. Just ﬁve dudes playing together through one pair of eyes, out-working, out-executing, and out-physicaling their opponents. Coach Moore would’ve loved them. And honestly, that’s been the story for the last 10 years — units earning it the hard way, just like he would’ve wanted. After 10 years of wear and tear, we ﬁgured the award deserved what most linemen avoid — a fresh cut. Thanks to Van Horn Brands, we gave it a crisp new logo and a cleaner look, but kept the grit right where it belongs. And while we were at it, we planted a ﬂag with a new mantra: Own The Trenches™. It’s already catching on in O-line rooms across the country, and this fall, we’ll drop an apparel line for anyone — any level, any era — who’s ever lowered their pads in a gotta-have-it moment, and wants to wear that pride on their chest. Truth is, this award has never been about me — or even just Coach Moore. It’s about all of us: the offensive linemen who grind for one another, the coaches who still teach it the right way, and the countless players, past and present, who have lived life in the trenches. The guys who have had to believe in themselves and deliver when it mattered most. It’s a tribute to every big man who has ever sacriﬁced personal glory for the good of the group. And it’s folks like Phil who help the rest of the football world see just how special this position really is. So here’s to the ﬁrst 10 years — and to whatever comes next. As long as there are ﬁve men willing to move other men against their will, the Joe Moore Award will be right there, owning the trenches. 7

2026 NFL DRAFT A DAY FOR VHT’s VHT’s By Phil Steele The NFL Draft is always a big day for the top graduating seniors, some high-quality juniors and a few third-year sophomores in college football. Colleges beneﬁt by having former players being drafted high as it allows them to use it to attract future recruiting classes. It is a chance for players to move on to the NFL and make a living playing the sport they have participated in for most of their lives. For ﬁrst-round draft picks, it means millions of dollars and sudden wealth. While lower round draft picks rarely make millions, everyone has the potential to earn a substantial income and that is why a big ﬁnal year in college is very important. Being a ﬁrst-round draft pick does not guarantee success. The NFL has many stories of ﬁrst round “busts” over the years, players who never lived up to their potential due to injuries or just poor performance. Every franchise has had a #1 pick who never panned out or who never even started an NFL game. However, the majority of ﬁrst round picks do make it big and have an impact on their team and the NFL. Ten seasons ago, supporters of Aaron Donald were concerned when he did very little in his ﬁrst 4 games with the Rams (just 9 tackles). However, the player that HC Jeff Fisher predicted would be the 2014 Defensive Rookie of the Year, took off from there logging 8 sacks in the Rams' ﬁnal 12 games (had 9 total sacks). That's more than Khalil Mack (4) and CJ Mosley (3) had combined as they ﬁnished #2 and #3 in the voting. Odell Beckham Jr single-handedly grabbed the Offensive Rookie of the Year Award despite missing his ﬁrst 4 games as he averaged 133 yards receiving in his ﬁrst 9 starts. How does a player get to be a ﬁrst-round draft pick? A good starting point in determining a player’s grade coming out of college is how that player performs on the ﬁeld. In most cases, you must be among the most productive players in the college game. However, productivity is not the only criteria. Former East Carolina walk-on Justin Hardy obliterated the FBS record for career receptions (349) and his 4,541 career yards were third overall, but he was selected in the 4th round of the 2015 Draft. Former Arizona Wildcats RB Ka'Deem Carey had 22 100-yard games in his ﬁnal two years of CFB and after being drafted by Chicago in the 4th round in 2015, only had 443 yards rushing in his ﬁrst 3 seasons. NFL scouts concentrate primarily on a player's size, speed and strength ratings. A player could have a great senior year, but if his performance in the 40-yard dash is disappointing, he could drop a round or two in the draft. If a player has a bad showing at the NFL Combine/Pro Day or has lingering medical/off-the-ﬁeld issues, he'll probably cost himself a large chunk of money as he will be drafted lower than expected. Alabama LB Reuben Foster was projected as a Top-10 draft choice, but after some questions regarding his injured shoulder along with an off-the-ﬁeld incident during the combine, he fell all the way back to the 31st overall pick in 2017. It’s all about how many reps a player can do at 225 pounds in the bench press, vertical jump, short shuttle and other measurable physical characteristics. Even after all the number crunching, there are numerous stories about players who were very late-round DC's or not even drafted who went on to have great success in the NFL. Tom Brady who became one of the best QB's of all time was just a 4th round pick. DE Cameron Wake joined the Dolphins back in '09 and was one of the NFL's best edge rushers since earning 5 Pro Bowl nods and posting 11.5 sacks in 4 different seasons. These stories are great, but the majority of the stars in the NFL are the players who were graded high enough to be upper-round draft picks. Colleges do not have a draft of high school players, but every school has an allotment of scholarships and has to recruit players from around the country to ﬁll their needs. Most high school athletes will take the big-name schools' scholarship offers over the smaller ones. If you are lucky enough to have Alabama, Georgia or Ohio St offer you one of their precious 15 to 25 scholarships, you usually jump at the opportunity. Many non-FBS schools do not even bother to recruit most of the top athletes coming out, as they really have little chance to land them (unless it’s a local prospect). Since there is no draft, how do you rate players out of high school? I rely on some great recruiting sources and have a computer rating system that ranks over 12,000 high school & junior college players each season. Then I assign every player a PS# which shows how highly rated each player is out of high school or JC. I have an entire page devoted to how I determine a PS# (see page 361). I've come up with my own terminology for the players' ratings out of high school on that page. An HT (Highly Touted) is a player who is rated highly at his position. Of the estimated 12,000 or so kids who are on my list coming out of high school each year, the top 1,445 fall into the HT category (about 12%). A VHT (Very Highly Touted) is similar to a ﬁrst-round draft pick. There are 584 of these players each year (about 5%), with varying amounts at each position. That comes out to just 11.7 players per state, so we're talking about the crème de la crème recruits. When a player moves into a college program, he beneﬁts from vastly upgraded weight rooms and nutritional programs. Players will show much greater gains in size, speed and strength in their 3 to 5 years in college than they do once an NFL team drafts them. For example, Cameron Erving was a 6-5 290-lb DL when he joined Florida St and was average at best with 21 tackles in 16 games on that side of the ball. He ﬂipped to the OL and won the Jacobs Blocking Trophy as an OL. In '15 the 6-6 308-lb OL tested at 30 reps, 9'3" broad jump and 7.48 3-cone drill prior to being drafted 19th by Cleveland. The recruiting ratings are not an exact science. However, much like the NFL, you will ﬁnd that the most sought after kids out of high school usually turn out to be the stars of the college game. There are many cases of VHT players stepping in and starting in their true freshmen seasons. This year, I again looked at the end product of the college game. In mid-May, after the 2026 NFL Draft was complete, I went back and looked at the PS#’s of all the 1st Round picks. For the eleventh straight year, 16 or more selections were VHT rated players who earned a ﬁrst-round selection. In the 2025 draft 21 of the 32 players 8 selected in the ﬁrst round were VHT's. In the 2024 draft 22 of 32 players drafted in the ﬁrst round were VHT's. In the 2023 draft, another 19 of 31 players drafted in the ﬁrst round were VHT's. In '22, 22 of 32 players drafted were VHT's. In '21, 17 of 32 were VHT's. In '17, 24 of the 32 draftees were VHT's, with no more than two consecutive selections occurring with players that were not VHT's (18 of the top 20 were VHT's). In '16, 22 of the 31 draftees were VHT's, and 15 of the Top 20 were VHT's. There are around 3,200 players who are signed to a scholarship by FBS schools each year. Since there are just 584 players who meet my criteria for a VHT, that means that roughly 18% of all signees are classiﬁed as a VHT. In the last 25 years, 202 of the 288 Top 12 picks in the draft have been VHT's! That means 70% of the top spots were VHT's which proves the signiﬁcance of the rating. Below is a list of this year's 1st Round NFL Draft selections and how they were rated out of high school. As you can see, the 2026 NFL Draft was another dominating VHT day. 2026's NFL DRAFT TOP SELECTIONS 1. Fernando Mendoza 2. David Bailey 3. Jeremiyah Love 4. Carnell Tate 5. Arvell Reese 6. PHIL STEELE’S DRAFT GUIDE Welcome to the Phil Steele Draft Guide. On this page are 221 players from my 2025 Draft Eligible Players. Overall 121 players were drafted, 41 players went undrafted and 54 opted to stay in college. Over the last ﬁfteen years 543 out of 620 (87.6%) undrafted players were given the chance to continue their careers playing football at the next level. Please note that we are not including players who retire due to medical issues as a miss as their health has priority. Check out my Top Draft Eligible Players on pages 12-14 and see who I think will be taken in 2027’s draft. In the past Eighteen years 283 of the 331 DE’s listed on this page that were seniors or declared early were either drafted or signed as a UFA with a team (85.5%). In that span 250 of 294 DT’s (85.0%) and 273 of 323 WR’s (84.5%) were also given a chance by an NFL team to continue their dreams. Also, since 2009 only ELEVEN players from the QB’s, CB’s or SS’s that did not return to school and were listed on this page were not drafted or signed as a UFA. Over the past 22 editions of this page of “Tops” there have been 4,600 players listed. There have been 3,602 players who were drafted or returned to school (78.3%) and 854 UFA’s (18.6%) signed. Only 144 players listed on these pages were not drafted, not signed as a free agent or did not return to their schools (3.1%). That’s 96.9% of players who earned the opportunity to compete for their dreams at the next level. Draft Day Party Hangover Draft day is a life changing experience for many college football players, as they ﬁnd out which professional team they will be playing for in the future. Many players who will be 1st or 2nd round draft picks have draft parties to celebrate their high selection and the upcoming riches they will receive from signing an NFL contract. Networks often broadcast from high proﬁle draftees' living rooms showing them celebrating when and where they get drafted. College football teams also enjoy draft day, as having players selected to the NFL gives coaches a future recruiting edge. They can then tell incoming high school recruits how many different players they have sent on to have NFL careers. Naturally, the more successful programs will always land the top-notch athletes who seek a pro career. While there is a lot of happiness on draft day, it can be a precursor for trouble for many college programs. My staff and I went back and researched how teams performed after having a large amount of players selected in the draft. We found almost 8 out of every 10 teams that rank among the top in the NCAA in players drafted, struggle the next year and have a weaker record. I call it the Draft Day Party Hangover. Let me explain how I came up with this theory. I have taken the last 29 drafts and analyzed not only the amount of players selected, but also the rounds in which they were selected. Let's face it, there are (usually) only 32 players in all of college football who end up being a 1st round draft pick in a season. Replacing a player with that ability is often very difﬁcult. For the system I created, 7 points are awarded if a player was picked in the 1st round. A 2nd round pick garners 5 points, a 3rd round pick 4 points, 4th round 3 points, and a 5th round 2 points. In the NFL there's not much difference between a 6th or 7th round pick and a high quality undrafted free agent signee, so I award 1 point to a 6th or 7th round pick. I do not lend a high level of merit to being picked in the last 2 rounds. Using this point system, I have plugged in the data for the last 29 years and found some interesting results. I limited my research to those teams that totaled 12 or more points, which makes them among the best in the NCAA. I do eliminate a team from my list that totaled 12 or more points if that is LESS than the previous year's total. There is no question some programs turn out numerous draft picks every year and 12 is a low total for some teams. Over the past 29 years I have gone through season-by-season and recapped how the teams that earned 12 or more points fared. The results have been VERY consistent. In the 29 years, there have been 509 teams that earned 12 or more points while having more points than what they earned the previous year. Of those 509 teams, 319 or 62.9% had a WEAKER record the next season and 49 had the same record (9.6%). Only 136 (26.7%) managed to improve their record. Last year 16 teams ﬁt the criteria and 5 (31.3%) managed to improve their record. It is only natural for teams to struggle as highly touted draft classes mature and move on. Recruiting is crucial to a program and only the best can replenish year in and year out. The strongest year for this system of NFL Draft Hangover was 1998 when 18 of the 21 teams had a weaker record the following season. Here are some examples of the teams that earned 12 points or more and how they have done from one year to the next. A great example in 2008, the 5 best examples were: Arizona St (13 pts), Auburn (18 pts), Kansas (14 pts), Purdue (14 pts), and Virginia (15 pts) as they combined for a 48-17 (74%) record in '07, but fell to a combined 27-34 (44%) in 2008 with 4 of the 5 having losing records! In 2010, Texas was coming off a 13-1 season, but after 6 players were drafted in the ﬁrst 4 rounds, they dropped to 5-7 for their ﬁrst losing season in the Mack Brown era. In 2011, the defending champ Auburn (16 pts) went from a 14-0 season to just 8-5. Ohio St (14 pts) went from 12-1 to 6-7, their most losses in a single season since 1897! For 2012, Arkansas (13 pts) went from 11-2 to a 4-8 season. In 2015, Missouri (24 pts) was coming off a Citrus Bowl win (11-3), but went 5-7 in 2016. During 2016, TCU dropped from being 11-2 (#7) to a 6-7 record. In 2017 Western Michigan lost 13 points, their most since 2005, and went from 13-1 to 6-6. In 2018 USC (21 pts), Louisville (19 pts), UCLA (21 pts), and Virginia Tech (19 pts) went from a combined 38-15 72% to a combined 20-30 40% with all 4 having a losing season. In 2022, Baylor (20 pts), Oklahoma (17 pts), and Texas A&M (17 pts) went from a combined 32-8 in 2021 to a combined 17-21. In the 2006 magazine I went through the records of teams in the chart and noticed that of the TOP 7 I had listed, ALL 7 had a weaker record in 2005! The 2006 results veriﬁed my theory that the more points a team earns (which means the bigger the draft losses), the higher chance they would have of a weaker record the next year. If you go back over the last 29 years, there have been 137 teams that have accumulated 24 or more points, an amount higher than the year before. Of those 137 teams, 102 had a weaker record the next year (11 had the same record). That means 102 of the 137 teams (74.5%) failed to improve their record the next year after earning 24 or more draft points. Here are some notable losers from this segment of draft casualties. In 2014, Florida (31 pts) went from 11-2 and a BCS bowl to just 4-8, their worst season since 1979. In 2012, Illinois went from 7-6 with a bowl win over UCLA to 2-10 and the worst record in the Big Ten! In 2004, Ohio St set an NFL record for the number of players drafted in a seven round draft (14) and in the process, earned 51 draft points in my system. It was quality over quantity in 2016 as their ﬁve 1st round draft choices (12 overall) helped them crush that mark with 63 draft points. By way of reference, the 2002 Hurricanes lost 49 points in their fantastic draft class. My next question is, how do the biggest draft losers fare the next season? In the past 27 years there have only been 34 teams that have earned 35 or more points with more points than the previous year. Twenty-four of 34 had a weaker record the next season with the 2006 Ohio St Buckeyes, 2008 USC Trojans, 2012 Alabama Crimson Tide, 2014 Florida St Seminoles, 2017 LSU Tigers, 2020 Alabama Crimson Tide and 2023 Alabama Crimson Tide being the only teams to have a better record. The biggest fall from this group was LSU, which went from 15-0 in 2019 to just 5-5 in 2020. In 2010, Florida had 45 points and went from 13-1 to 8-5. In 2020 Clemson earned 30 points on draft day but that was less than they lost in 2019 when they lost 31 points so they did not qualify. As it was, Clemson went from 14-1 to 10-2, but also went from National Champs to losing to Ohio St in the semiﬁnal. Over the last 29 years, teams that earned more points than the previous year and accumulated... 12 or more points - Weaker or same record 368 of 509 (72.3%) 24 or more points - Weaker or same record 105 of 137 (76.6%) 35 or more points - Weaker record 31 of 42 (73.8%) It's interesting to note how many teams in a conference have made the list this year. 16 out of 16 teams for this year's list are from Power 4 conferences with Seven SEC, Four Big Ten, Three ACC and Two Big 12 teams. One thing I have pointed out in past seasons is that the National Champ does have a good shot at appearing on these lists. In the past 28 years there have been 29 National Champs (LSU and USC were co-champs in 2003) with 24 of the 29 having earned 12 or more points in the draft the previous year. The exceptions were in 2006 (Florida, 7 pts), 2008 (Florida, 11 pts), 2010 (Auburn, 7 pts), and 2018 where Clemson only earned 6 points and 2025 Indiana earned 4 points. According to past history, only 4 or 5 teams will manage to improve their record this year. Take a look at the box below. Is your favorite team on this list? LINEBACKERS 2026’s Top LB Units 1. Notre Dame - Notre Dame’s biggest issue this year at LB will be keeping everyone happy. Four different players started at least 2 games last year, led by Drayk Bowen and Jaiden Ausberry. Jaylen Sneed (PS#8) and Kyngston Viliamu-Asa (PS#5) would start for most schools across the country. 2. LSU - The Tiger defense got a huge boost with the return of Whit Weeks who missed time last year but was an All-American in 2024. He’ll be joined by a pair of 90+ tacklers, Ole Miss transfer TJ Dottery and Davhon Keys who led LSU in tackles a season ago. 3. Texas - Sark scored a massive portal win with the addition of Rasheem Biles (101 tkls, 17 tﬂ last year at Pitt). The Horns also added 8-gm starter Justin Cryer from Florida St and PS#1 Tyler Atkinson to go along with VHT Ty’Anthony Smith as the projected starter at MLB. 4. Oklahoma - The Sooners welcome back last year’s top 2 tacklers, Kip Lewis and Owen Heinecke, from a stout defense that held opponents 107 yards below their season average. OU also added Michigan VHT Cole Sullivan to provide support and competition to Heinecke in the middle. 5. Georgia - The Dawgs are once again littered with play making VHTs at the second level. Raylen Wilson and Chris Cole are experienced veterans with NFL futures, and STAR Khalil Barnes was a terriﬁc pickup from Clemson. Georgia’s top 3 are as good as anyone in the country. 6. Tennessee - Three of last year’s top 4 tacklers are returning linebackers, Arion Carter, Edwin Spillman and Jeremiah Telander. BYU - The addition of Cade Uluave from Cal took an already good unit to an entirely different level. Ole Miss - The Rebels addressed their turnover at the position with the strategic additions of Baylor’s Keaton Thomas (2nd Tm All-Big 12 last year) and Cal’s Luke Ferrelli (4th Tm All-ACC last year). The staff believes this is their best group of linebackers since they’ve been at Ole Miss. 9. Texas Tech - HC McGuire has always been impressed by the play Austin Romaine so he plucked him out of Kansas St and added him to Ben Roberts (3rd Tm All-Big 12 last year) and STAR John Curry who might have the highest NFL ceiling on the entire Red Raider defense. 10. Clemson - Junior Sammy Brown is living up to his PS#2 hype after making 107 tkls and earning 1st Tm All-ACC last year (his ﬁrst as a full-season starter). Penn St - New HC Campbell thinks this is the best linebacker room he’s coached which is ﬁtting at LB U. STOCK MARKET INDICATOR by Phil Steele Metrics, Metrics, Metrics. In 2012, I produced my ﬁrst Stock Market Indicator article and it has delivered solid results each year. In 2012, Ohio St had a Stock Market Indicator (SMI) of +5.5, which would be a Bull Market. The +5.5 was calculated by taking their average win total from 2009-2010, which was 11.5 (11-2 in ’09, 12-1 in ’10), then subtracting their wins from ‘11 (just 6) which produced the +5.5. The Buckeyes clearly under performed in ‘11 and were poised for a big bounce back the next year (Bull Market). My Stock Market Indicator proved to be spot on as the Buckeyes were the Most Improved Team in the country going 12-0 in ’12! In ‘13, Auburn was coming off a 3-9 season following two years of going a combined 22-5. That earned them a +8 in my Stock Market Indicator and they got to the National Title game! In 2014, TCU was +5 in the Bull Market and went from 4-8 to 12-1 as the Most Improved Team in the country! In 2016, UCF was an amazing +10.5 in the Bull Market and improved from 0-12 to earning a bowl bid. The last eight years 103 teams have made the Bull Market box and 78 (76%) have improved their record! The Bear Market has also been a very accurate indicator. Over the last 9 years 92 teams have made the Bear Market box and only 19 have managed to improve their record just 21%. NCAA EXPERIENCE CHART This list is accurate through 6/5/26. Here is the formula. First is a tabulation of the Senior starters in the two deep (not counting P/K) along with Jr’s, Soph and Frosh. Then there is a count of returning lettermen % for each team. The percentage of yards is the tally of all the passing, rushing and receiving yardage combined that returns from the previous season. The % tackles adds up after going through the entire defense to determine who returns and gives an idea of experience there. The OL career starts factors in the trench aspects and while the players are not included in the overall stats they are a vital part of any offense. In 2021 I added Big plays on Defense (Sacks, TFL, Int’s). A master formula blends these factors together into a total number of 100 to 0. A perfect 100 would be a team with 25 Seniors (NCAA scholarship limit) in the two deep, every yard, tackle, sack, tﬂ and int returning and 120+ career OL starts. A 0 would be a team with no experience and no seniors in the two deep. The ﬁrst number is where each team ranks in the entire NCAA. The bolded teams are those that were bowl eligible last year so you can get a feel for those who may struggle or pull a surprise early in the season. This year on philsteele.com I will update this chart but also provide a chart that accounts for transfer player stats if a transfer player has earned a starting job after spring at their new school! This will be available on the July 15th daily blog & you can compare charts! Close Wins, Close Losses By Phil Steele Give me a computer full of NCAA football statistics and an entire offseason and I'm always going to try and uncover something new. Regular readers of my magazine know that I like to analyze what happens if a team was fortunate and won a lot of close games. Those teams are probably not as fortunate the next year, but on the ﬂip side, teams that suffered many close losses the previous year are generally undervalued. I now have 25 years of data from teams that had close wins and losses (games decided by a touchdown or less). I break it down further by ranking net close wins and losses. For example: In 2015, Michigan St beneﬁtted from 6 close wins with 1 close loss (5 net close wins) and went from a record of 12-2 to 3-9 the following year! In 2016, Notre Dame had 1 close win and 6 close losses, ﬁnishing with 5 net close losses and went from 4-8 to 10-3 in 2017. While I use a 7 points or less as the standard for a close win and loss, if there is a late misleading score, I will either include or exclude it accordingly. An example being that, Temple down 3. was at the 1 and UConn got a 96 yd fumble return TD :00 to win by 9 (did not kick xp). I count that as a close win. If a team is down 10 and scores a garbage TD on the last play to lose by 3, I do not count that as a close loss. Here is a chart showing the results from the last 25 years. In the last eight years, 123 teams had 3 Net Close Losses or more and 95 improved their record while 13 remained the same! I modiﬁed the chart for 2020 to account for uneven games which created some decimal points but we have been back to normal since 2021. Upset Meter: A few years ago, I was wondering if there was any value in predicting future success/failure for teams that pulled off a bunch of upsets the year prior and on the flip side, teams that were upset numerous times in the previous year. My hypothesis going into my research was that teams that pulled many upsets the previous year would be overvalued and see their record get weaker the following year, as teams would take them more seriously and the experts in Las Vegas would adjust their lines. Similarly, teams that were upset numerous times as favorites the previous year would be undervalued and would see their record improve. The results coincided with my original predictions as in the last 37 years, teams that pulled 3 or more NET upsets (upset wins minus upset losses) the previous year, have seen their record get weaker or stay the same 186 out of 259 times (71.8%). On the opposite end, teams that had a -3 or more net upsets the previous year have seen their record improve or stay the same on 181 out on 275 occasions for a 65.8% success rate. Check out PhilSteele.com right now (blog archive) to see what teams had a +3 or more net upset rating in '25 and will likely see their record get weaker and what teams who had a -3 or more upset rating in '25 will see their record improve! I put this article in for the ﬁrst time in 2004 & it continues to be an accurate forecaster of whether a team will record will ﬁnish with a stronger or weaker record the next year. First of all, let me explain what YPP is exactly. A YPP is simply yards By Phil Steele per point. An offense is more efﬁcient when their YPP is a lower number. If a team had an offensive YPP of 10.0, that would mean for every 200 yards gained, they scored 20 points. Meanwhile, if they had an offensive YPP of 20.0, then for every 200 yards gained, they only scored 10 points. Defenses want to have a higher YPP. Inverting the same thought, if a team allowed 200 yards and had a 20.0 YPP, that means they would allow just 10 points for every 200 yards the opposition traveled, whereas a 10.0 YPP would be 20 points for every 200 yards allowed. When I started this research in 1990, the average YPP for a team was 15.44. With all the rule changes slanted to the offense, it is no surprise that the median has dropped signiﬁcantly since then (13.9 in '15, 13.87 '20, 14.1 '21, 13.9 '23, 14.3 '24). I found teams that had a high Offensive YPP (move the ball but do not score) the previous year generally have a stronger record the next season. Let's look at teams that had an unusually high YPP the previous year (an inefﬁcient offense). If you look at the chart below you will see that 36 teams have had a YPP greater than 22.4 since 1990 and ALL 36 have had a stronger or identical record the next year. The chart goes to 16.6, which still has a solid success record, as teams will either have the same or a stronger record 73.6% of the time. UMass set an all-time record with a remarkably bad 62.5 Off YPP in '20! Northwestern was the lone +22.4 qualiﬁer in '23 with 0 the L/2 years. Of the teams with the seven weakest schedules in 2020 (my preseason rankings), all seven were bowl-eligible, with the seven teams combining for a record of 36-12 (75%) on the season! The yellow box above lists the strength of each team's regular season schedule for 2025. Note that the teams saddled with the nine hardest schedules all had disappointing seasons and the teams with the easiest six schedules had successful years relatively speaking. Now let’s turn our attention to 2026. Let’s ﬁrst look at the NCAA rankings. To the right is a chart of all 138 teams and the combined 2025 opponents' records. It is ranked in order of highest % of opponents' wins (or toughest schedule) to lowest % of opponents' wins (or easiest schedule). These rankings take two major factors into account. The ﬁrst is my nine sets of Power Ratings. This ensures that an FCS team is rated much lower than Florida which was just 4-8 last year. The second factor is the amount of home and away games played. As an example, this year some teams will have as many as eight home games, while others play as many as eight on the road. 28

TURNOVERS = DNUORANRUT Turnovers can have a huge impact on games and on a team's season. They can also lead to many misleading ﬁnal scores BY PHIL STEELE and make or break a season. This article was in my very ﬁrst magazine back in 1995 and really got me hooked on uncovering different metrics to help me forecast how teams will fare the next year. That year I went back and looked at three years worth of information on teams that had double-digit turnovers the previous year. The data from those three years showed that teams that beneﬁtted from double-digit turnovers one year had a weaker or the same record 75% of the time. The opposite was true for teams off a season with a negative double-digit turnover ratio also with a 75% success rate. That ﬁrst magazine was just 192 pages and printed on black and white newsprint. There have been many changes in the world since 1995 and a lot of changes with the magazine, which is now full color and almost double the size. There has been one constant over the 32 years and that is the results of the Turnovers Equals Turnaround article which continues to hit at least 70% on a yearly basis. If anything, the results are getting stronger as the last fourteen years 87 teams have beneﬁtted from +14 turnovers or more. The next season they had the weaker or same record 85% of the time. The last three years 26 teams made the Going Up Box and only one of the 26 had a weaker record for a success rate of 96%! The last two years 40 teams have made the Going Down box and only 11 improved their record. In the last eight years there have been 85 teams in the Going Up Box. Only 15 of those teams had a weaker record the next year with the box going 60-15-10. In 2023 Arizona St was -11 in turnovers and went from 3-9 to the College Football Playoff!. The last 8 years there were 80 teams in the Going Down box and 55 had a weaker record. That means the Going Up and Going Down boxes combined have gone 115-34-16 the last 7 years, a success rate of 79.4%. Turnovers can have a signiﬁcant impact on games as well during a team's season. They can also lead to many misleading ﬁnal scores. In '24 Pitt was +5 in TO's and blasted Syracuse 41-13! The next week an undefeated Pitt coming off a misleading ﬁnal was thumped by SMU on the road by SMU 48-25. Syracuse coming off a misleading loss upset Virginia Tech at home. Each week on my Phil Steele Plus Tour with selections, I will give you a Misleading Final play of the week for free (see page 11) and usually 6-8 other free plays with complete reasoning. This is the article that got me going on all the different metrics that I use in the magazine. What turned out to be 3 years of research has now grown into 36 years (90-'25). This is the 32nd year for this article and it has been a proven winner each year of the magazine. Here are this year's Turnaround teams. Allow me to shed some light on the great debate over which conference is the toughest. One of the most exciting things about college football is that the top conference can change on a yearly basis. In fact, even the SEC, synonymous with league supremacy, was dethroned in 2016, 2017, 2024 and 2025! Previously, the SEC was virtually untouchable, winning National Championships eight times from 2006-2015, as well as the top spot in my ﬁnal Toughest Conference Ratings a remarkable nine consecutive years. The SEC has not only not won a national title the last 3 years, they have not had a team in the National Title game in the last 3 years! Heck, I recall back in the late 1960's, when it could have been argued that the Southwest Conference stood atop college football, with powerhouses like Arkansas and Texas duking it out for #1. Some fans of unbeaten Penn State are annoyed to this day that President Nixon proclaimed the Horns were #1 after beating the Hogs in the 1969 "Game of the Century." In later years, it was the Big 8, headlined by Nebraska and Oklahoma dominating the landscape. Naturally, the SEC never strays far from the top. Ditto for the Big Ten. Both conferences have had their glory years that conjure up fond memories of Bear Bryant's Tide and the storied ten year rivalry pitting Ohio State's Woody Hayes vs Michigan's Bo Schembechler. There have been a lot of conference face-lifts over the past 20 years, with the realignments spawning some major power shifts. Another interesting point is that there's no exact science for selecting college football's premier conference. There's no relying, for instance, on how many bowl wins a league racks up or on its overall record in non-conference play. Let's face it, some leagues' non-conf slates are signiﬁcantly thornier than others. Some teams traditionally fatten up on FCS opponents, so a strict adherence to win-loss record is not enough. Before diving into the 2026 pecking order, let's look at the results from the previous decade for a historical reference. As always, I've accounted for all of the factors in my calculations (non-conference record, record vs Power 4 (was 5), average power ratings, and bowl records) to rank the conferences. In 2016, a new king was crowned. The ACC, which was ﬁfth a year earlier, shot up to #1 on the strength of non-conf success. The ACC was the only league with a winning record vs Power 5 teams (16-10) and it won by far the most bowl games (9), including ﬁve over ranked teams. The SEC maintained its dominance on draft day and produced ﬁve Top 25 schools, but it wasn't enough. The top four conferences of 2016 were: #1 ACC, #2 SEC, #3 Pac-12 and #4 Big Ten. In 2017, the Big Ten earned the top spot, the third different league to wear the crown in three years. In a tight race, the Big Ten pulled away in December and January, going 7-1 in the bowls (four wins over ranked teams). On the ﬂip side, the Pac-12 went 1-8 in bowls and sunk to ﬁfth among the P5 schools. The SEC was still a close second in the race. The top four conferences of 2017 were: #1 Big Ten, #2 SEC, #3 Big 12 and #4 ACC. In 2018, the SEC did not win the National Title, as Clemson of the ACC took home that honor. However, the ACC managed just two ranked teams (14%) at the end of the year. The SEC had four Top 10 teams and six overall in the Top 25. The Big 12 did well with 3 of their 10 teams (30%) ranked while the Big Ten had 5 ranked teams (36%). Only 3 conferences had a winning record vs Power 5 non-conf foes during the regular season. The SEC was #1 at 9-3, the Big Ten was 7-5, while the Independents were 12-10. Clemson was 2-0 vs P5 non-conf schools in the regular season but the rest of the ACC was just 2-9. The SEC dominated in the draft pick category and had 3 wins over Top 10 teams in the bowls. The top four of 2018 were: #1 SEC, #2 Big Ten, #3 Big 12 and #4 ACC. In 2019 in the preseason, I had the Pac-12 moving up to the #3 spot after two straight years as the #5 Power 5 league. The Pac-12 nearly had a team qualify for the playoff and did go 9-8 vs other P5 leagues including the bowls and ﬁnished #3. The SEC was the runaway winner with the National Champion in LSU and an 8-2 bowl record and four Top 10 teams at the end. The 2019 season was the ﬁrst year that a Group of 5 league topped a Power 5 league in my ratings as the American Conference (AAC) topped the ACC for the #5 league! The American ﬁnished with four ranked teams and the ACC had just one in Clemson! The top 4 conferences were: #1 SEC, #2 Big Ten, #3 Pac-12 and #4 Big 12 In 2020 the Big 10, SEC, Pac-12 and MAC all played conference-only schedules, so we did not have the usual non-conference records to compare. The opening week the Sun Belt went 3-0 vs the Big 12 but the Big 12 won their other 6 non-conf games. The ACC and CUSA went a futile 0-6 in bowl games! Notre Dame was an ACC member and the ACC had two Top 10 teams at the end. The Sun Belt went 4-1 in bowls and had two ranked teams at the end. The Big 12 ﬁnished with 4 ranked teams tying the SEC. First, let me explain how I derive the results. I complete nine primary sets of power ratings at the start of the year. First is a pure power rating. I rank the positions (QB, RB, WR, etc) from 4 to 10 points. I then add up all of the positions, factor in coaching and special teams, and derive my Power Rating for each team. The second Power Plays Rating is based on my Computer Ratings (see page 43), which takes into account the team's production not only in terms of points, but also yards gained and allowed. I compile a detailed list of areas of improvement and spots that are weaker and either upgrade or downgrade each team's Offense/Defense numbers. I then add up all the different numbers and get my Preseason Computer Ratings number for each team. Three other sets are based on last year's ﬁnal numbers. I grade every position for each team (QB, RB, WR, OL, DL, LB, DB) on their scale of improvement from one year to the next. The scale ranges from +6 points to -6 points for each position. I take the total team number and factor it into last year's 3 ﬁnal sets of Power Ratings including the Plus/Minus Ratings (pg 34). This gives me 3 very different ways of gauging the strength of the teams. So how do I add up the points? Conferences all have a different number of teams. If I ranked them by the average of the entire conference, that would give a good indication of the average rating of all the teams. But the bigger the league, the weaker the grade could possibly be. I did use that as a factor. I then added a second factor, the average grade of just the Top 5 teams. This would give me an even comparison of all the leagues. The only thing this rating doesn't show, of course, is overall depth. For example, let's say one conference had nine bowlcaliber teams and one non-bowl team and another conference had ﬁve bowl-caliber teams and ﬁve non-bowl teams. The thinner conference would be rated higher if the Top 5 teams had a higher average, even though the deeper conference was likely tougher. I also rate leagues by the Top 3 and Top 8. By merging four ratings, I get an accurate assessment of conference strength. Basically, after all of that is done, I have four different ranking sets. They break down the conferences based upon the strength of the top TOUGHEST 3 teams in each conference, the top 5 teams, CONFERENCE the top 8 teams, and then FOR the overall strength of the whole conference. 1. WHO WILL BE THIS YEAR'S SURPRISE TEAM? By Phil Steele What is the deﬁnition of a Phil Steele surprise team? A "Surprise Team" is a NON Preseason AP Top-10 team that I think has a decent shot at making the playoff and even winning the national championship. In 2000, Oklahoma entered the year #22 in the AP poll and was a 50-1 long shot to win the national title that season. When the dust cleared the Sooners were the only undefeated team in the FBS (115 teams that season) and were crowned National Champions. That win by Oklahoma had me start this article in 2001, which back then had the headline "Who Will be this Year's Oklahoma?" Listed on the next two pages is a recap of each year and how I graded them. Let me talk about the grades. Now I am a math guy and back in school whenever I took a math test any grade that came back lower than an A was unacceptable. Math is black and white, there is a right answer and a wrong answer. A perfect score is very achievable. I should also mention I have zero artistic talent and can barely draw a stick ﬁgure, so I won't mention my grades in art class. Math may be black and white but sports and predicting the future are not. Babe Ruth was the greatest home run hitter of all time. He was hitting 40 or 50 home runs in a era when entire teams did not hit that many in a season combined. As great as the Babe was he only hit a home run 8.5% of the time he came to bat and struck out 15.8% of the time. Quarterbacks complete anywhere from 40% to 70% of their passes. Completing 40% would be worth a D or F and 70% would rate an A+. However, 70% would not rate an A on a math test. Predicting the future can be tough (ask any weatherman). In football (or any sport) you do not have knowledge of how injuries, key fumbles or mistakes, referee calls or other uncontrollable things will factor into play during the year. NFL teams do as thorough of a job as possible breaking down each quarterback for the upcoming NFL draft, before picking one in the ﬁrst round. Somehow, over half of those ﬁrst-round draft pick QB's do not pan out with very few becoming the franchise QB the team was hoping for when they made their selection. OK, we have established that football and predicting the future can not be held to the same grading scale as a math test. In years past I spent a full paragraph breaking down what happened each year to my Surprise Teams, but this year I decided to make it a lot easier to read and have given you just a brief summary of each year and the grade I assigned for the year. I am sure most of you have an old copy of the magazine from previous years that you can refer to if you need a more detailed version of each season. In 2022 I noted I was coming off probably the roughest year for a Surprise Team (see notes) and called for a bounce back year. USC was off a 4-8 season was my #2 Surprise Team and came within one game of making the playoff. Two quick notes. With this type of success through the years, you might think that it is very easy to select teams that had losing records the previous year and have become bowl eligible the next season. I went back to 1992 and took a look at all of the teams that ﬁnished with losing records in a season. In that span, there have been 1,685 teams that ﬁnished with a record below .500. Of those 1,685 teams, only 514 of them managed to ﬁnish ABOVE .500 the next year, which comes out to just 30.5%. Teams now play a 12 game regular season, so a 6-6 record equals bowl eligibility. To be fair, out of the 1,685 teams an additional 84 were bowl eligible the next year. So of the 1,685 teams, only 590 (35.0%) managed to go from a losing record to at least .500 the next year. The combined record of all the teams which had a losing record from 1992-2014 was 4009-9269 or 30.2%. The next year those same teams showed a slight overall improvement in their records to 5412-8207, or just 39.7%. So on average, a team that had a losing season in that span improved by 9.5% over the previous year's record. Naturally, the teams I feel are the most improved are in my Top 10. My Top Ten Most Improved Teams over the last 22 years had a combined record of 1164-1956 (37.3%) the previous year and improved to 1799-1475 (55%) the next year. That is DOUBLE the normal improvement for teams with losing records. In the last 22 years, I have had a total of 416 teams on my MIT List. Of the 416 teams that made my Most Improved List in the last 22 years, 341 (82.4%) have won at least the same amount of games as the previous year or have improved their win total. Over the last 16 years, I have listed 289 teams on my MIT List that did not have a winning season the previous year. Almost all improved their record the next year, but even more impressively, 195 of the 289 teams were bowl eligible the next year which is 67.4% and the from '21-'24 48 of the 64 teams 75% MADE a BOWL! The grade represents not only how much the team won by or how much they outgained an opponent by but it's also compared to what my computer forecasted. Both teams in a game are graded on their offensive and defensive performances in rushing, passing, scoring as well as taking into account homefield advantage (or lack of), TO’s and the actual quality of the foe in the game. That’s why you don’t see many “big school vs little school” blowouts here. Quality matters on both sides of the field!!! Navy POWER POLL TOP 138 As I clearly point out in the front of the magazine, MY College Top-40 is based solely on where I think each team will FINISH and NOT how I rate the teams talent-wise. I stress each year that my Surprise Teams are often teams that not only have decent talent but a GREAT schedule. An example from this year is Boise St, who is just #47 in my Power Poll but is #15 in my Preseason Top-40 Article (page 49), as they face my #85 toughest schedule (page 29) and should have a winning year. On the other side, Wisconsin is #32 in my Power Poll but is not ranked in my Preseason Top-40 as the Badgers face the nation’s #1 toughest schedule. To come up with the order for this article, I could have continued on from teams I list in my Top 40 article and extended the list to #136 using that method. However, the weakest teams listed in my Top 40 may be those that faced the toughest schedules, so I did not feel that would be a fair representation. Therefore, I decided to give you my Power Poll Top-138. Let me explain why I call it the Power Poll and how it was derived. A number of years back, before computers became part of the then-BCS rankings system, there was without a doubt some ﬂaws in the polls. Some teams rated #2 or #3 in the country really were not that talented and were maybe only the 5th or 6th best. One internet site decided to produce a poll of some of the top analysts and experts each week and invited me to join. I myself work 365 days a year on one thing, FOOTBALL. During magazine time (January thru June this year) and throughout the football season (August through December) there are many 15-18 hour days put in and all of them are spent solely working on FOOTBALL. When they invited me to join the poll, I wanted to give them the best set of power ratings in the country to help make the poll as accurate as possible. The dilemma I had was which set? As I mention throughout the magazine, I now have NINE sets of power ratings that are based on different factors. For example, one is based on the individual talent level and performance of each position on each team and those are totaled up for the rating. Another is based on my computer numbers which include rushing & passing offenses, defenses and special teams. Another is a continually updated power rating based on the score of the games and the strength of opponent played. What I decided to do was combine all nine into one rating which gives me a very solid overall ranking for each team. The rating takes into account EVERY factor, using it as my main set of power ratings. These numbers will differ from my “Plus or Minus” ratings on page 32 as that set is just ONE of my NINE used to compile this main number. As mentioned earlier, these numbers will differ from my Top-40 because the Power Poll is concerned ONLY with the STRENGTH of the TEAM and does not factor in who they will play for the upcoming season or how many games they should win in 2025. Keep in mind, this is basically MY COMPUTER’S Top-138 and is based on the overall talent of each team. Here is my 2026 Power Poll ranking the teams 1-138. OREGON #2 NEVADA #112 46 70. Stanford 71. CONF YPG VS. CONF RECORD Conference YPG vs Conference Record – Which teams are going up/down this year? I have been tracking the Conference YPG vs conference record from 2001 all the way through this past year so I have 25 years of research invested in this Metric. It seems like right now a lot of people use Metrics. Way back in 1995, I put the ﬁrst Metric article (Metrics was not a term back then) into the magazine and it was Turnovers = Turnaround. That article had ﬁve years of research put into it and has stayed true to form with now 36 years of research into it and remains a 75% accurate indicator of teams either going up or down the next season. Since that ﬁrst article, I have added a bunch of Metrics to the magazine. While I have referred to the Conference YPG in plenty of team write-ups, I have never put the actual article into my magazine, but it has had great success. My hypothesis behind the metric were that teams that outgained their conference foes but ﬁnished with a losing record were much better than their record and would likely improve the next season. On the ﬂip side, teams that were outgained but caught a lot of breaks and ﬁnished with a winning record would be overvalued and likely have a weaker record the next year. I am a math guy and I had to come up with a formula to ﬁgure out how many yards translated into wins and or losses. Studying the many years of previous standings, I came up with 35 yards per game (ypg) per win above .500. My formula took the total ypg divided by the 35 ypg I credited for each game above .500 on the season and then added in half of the games played. As an example, a team that was 0 ypg on the year and played an eight-game schedule should have four wins on the year. {0/35= 0+4 (for half the games played)}. If a team played an eight-game schedule and went 8-0 they should be +140 ypg. If a team went 6-2, they should be +70 ypg. If a team played a nine-game schedule than +52.5 ypg would be the mark for a 6-3 season and a 9-0 season would be if a team was +158 ypg. It works the same for negative ypg which translates into losing record. In an eight-game schedule you would start with 4 wins (0 ypg) and then add in the negative number. If a team was -105 ypg and would be -3 or just 1 win for the season is what they should have achieved. Let me give you some numbers from past years so you get an understanding of how this Metric works. In 2023 Washington made it to the National Title game and was undefeated in Pac 12 play but were outgained during the regular season in conference play! That rated them a -4.65 on the YPG metric and they fell to 6-7 and a losing year! New Mexico St rated a -2.5 and went from 10-5 to 3-9! At the top of the chart in 2024 Illinois was 5-7 and just 3-6 in Big Ten play but outgained their Big Ten foes by 26 ypg rating a +2/25 and they went from 5-7 to doubling their wins a 10-3! In 2022 some teams that were at the top of the YPG chart in the Going up Box were USC, Arizona and South Alabama. USC was just 4-8 in 2021 but they were actually +38 ypg in conference play! They rated a +2.58 and went 11-3! Arizona was 1-11 in 2021 but were just -17 ypg and rated a +3.01 in the YPG metric. They improved to 5-7 in 2022. South Alabama was just 5-7 in 2021 but were +30 ypg in Conference play and rated a +2.85 and improved to 10-3 in 2022! In 2021 Michigan St was the star of this metric. Somehow, someway in 2021 they went 11-2 despite being -63 ypg in Big Ten play rating a -4.28 in this metric and they went just 5-7 in 2022! In 2020 Tulsa was at the top of the Going Up Box for this metric. Tulsa was a poor 2-6 in conference play in 2019 but was only -5 ypg. Tulsa rated a +3.29 in my Conference YPG vs Wins. The next year in 2020 they were in the AAC title game vs Cincinnati. At the opposite end of the spectrum, Baylor was 8-1 in the Big 12 but only +23 ypg in 2019 which would be more indicative of a .500 year. The next year in 2020 Baylor went just 2-7. In 2019 Florida Atlantic was at the top of the Going Up Box for this metric. FAU was +87 ypg in CUSA play in 2018 but just 3-5 in conference play. That had them at a +3.5 in my Conference YPG vs Wins metric. The next year in 2020, FAU went 7-1 in CUSA play and won the conference. At the bottom of the metric was Northwestern. The Wildcats were an AMAZING 8-1 in conference play in 2018, but were ACTUALLY -43 ypg in Big Ten Play! The next year Northwestern rated a -4.3 in this metric and while they had similar yards at -58 ypg their record ended up just 1-8 for a major step back. In 2018 Baylor was near the top of the charts at +2.4 as they were 1-8 in Big 12 play in 2017 but only -40 ypg and in 2018 Baylor improved to 7-6 overall and 4-5 in conference play. Akron rated a -4.7 on my Conference YPG vs Wins metric as in 2017 they were 6-3 in MAC play but did it with mirrors as they were outgained by 103 ypg in conference play. As you would expect, the next year Akron tumbled to 2-6 in the MAC and 4-8 overall. In 2017 Michigan St was at the top of the Going Up box as in by Phil Steele 2016 the Spartans were +35 ypg in conference play but not only ﬁnished with a losing record but were 1-8!! My Conference YPG vs Wins metric at a +4.5 and as you would expect the Spartans were much better in 2017 as they were from 3-9 overall to 10-3 and 7-2 in Conference play. Georgia Tech was in the Going Down Box for 2017 as in 2016 the Yellow Jackets were 9-4 overall but were -86 ypg in Conference play. In 2017 Georgia Tech dropped to 5-6 overall. In 2023 Florida State was near the top of the chart as they were #1 in the ACC with +165 ypg but only ﬁnished with a 5-3 conference record so they graded a +3.7 and they ran the table and had an unbeaten season. Iowa State was just 4-8 in 2022 but were +52 ypg in conference play so they rated a super +4.99 on the YPG chart! The Cyclones improved to 7-6. TCU was near the bottom of the chart with a grade of -2.38 and they went from playing in the national title game to a losing season at 5-7 . Here is the chart for how this metric has done: Since 2001 there have only been six teams rated at -4.5 or lower and of those 6 teams, ﬁve had a weaker record the next year. Now you know I think Bill Snyder was one of the greatest head coaches of all time. Somehow in 2011 his Kansas St Wildcats were -107 ypg yet, 6-2 in Big 12 play. That rated them a -6.051. The next year somehow Snyder had them 8-1 in the Big 12 including a win over Texas in the Big 12 title game to be the only team to buck the metric at that level. In 2024 there was a rare qualiﬁer for that category in Washington which went 9-0 in the Pac 12 but were outgained during the regular season in conference play and rate a -4.65! Teams that are -2 or more have had a weaker or the same record 173 of 232 times for 74.1%. As you see on the chart the percentages work out perfectly with the records for teams in the negative category getting weaker as the negative points rise. Last year I listed the Going Up Box and the Going Down Box on this page. The teams in the Going Up Box had a 5-2-2 record with 5 teams improving, two having weaker and 2 having the same record as the previous year. The Going down box had an even better record with 9 teams having a weaker record and 3 improving which was right at the 75% accuracy that these boxes normally have. Marshall went from 10-3 to 5-7 and Colorado St went from 8-5 to 2-10. Here are the teams that make this year’s GOING UP BOX and GOING DOWN BOXES. These teams only have a 75% chance of improving their record if in the Going Up Box and having a weaker record if in the Going Down Box! returning starter box here in year 32 of the magazine. The style of the box and where it was positioned on the page has changed thru the years but it has mostly contained the Returning Starters with a Single number for Offense and Defense and the Returning Lettermen. Returning lettermen used to be a stat every school supplied and prior to the transfer portal era was a solid number in helping determine the experience of a team. Hardly any schools track this number any more and with so much roster turnover and new players coming in the stat has become insignificant. I have upgraded the box this year with even more information and the new chart is shown to the right. Not having Returning Lettermen listed is the first change. The second is having TWO numbers for the returning starters. The first number is overall Offensive or Defensive starters this year then a slash and the second number is how many starters are actually back from last years team. If a transfer player was a a starter for an FBS team last year and won the job in the spring, I count him as a returning starter but they have to have won the job. On the left hand pages you will see the players that are classified as a returning starter if My computer nails the weekly forethey are in ALL CAPS. As an example if a team has 6 starters back from last years team and added 2 transfers that were starters for casts each year. You can get my another FBS team and they won jobs the number would be 8/6 with 8 being the total starters and 6 starters being from last years team. On computers weekly forecast in my offense if a number has an * that means the QB is returning. Inside the pressbox Newsletter The Portal starts have a slash but on Added only. The first numCheckout PG 53 for Details or ber is FBS starts added and the second number is FCS starts added. Naturally all players lost are FBS starts lost as they are an FBS team. GEORGIA BULLDOGS QB GUNNER STOCKTON POSITION OUTLOOK FOR 2026 QUARTERBACKS - In '23 the Bulldogs had to replace their long time starter (4,127, 68%, 27-7, 205 rush) who was fourth in the Heisman voting. Carson Beck (PS#6) hit 72% (3941, 24-6) in his first year and threw for 3,485 (65%, 28-12) in '24 but he left for Miami. Gunner Stockton (PS#2) is a dangerous dual threat QB that led the comeback in the SEC title game but struggled vs ND. He threw for 440 (70%, 1-1) and added the QB run to the offense. Ryan Puglisi (PS#14) and true frosh Ryan Montgomery (PS#12) were the backups. I said Stockton should have a solid first year as a starter with an upgraded WR room. Stockton was one of the most clutch QBs last year at his best in the 4Q, on 4th down or when trailing. He threw for 2,894 yards (70%, 24-5) with 462 rush (3.6). He returns and will be a Heisman contender. RUNNING BACKS - In '24 the Bulldogs had to replace their #1 (880, 5.3) and #2 (790, 6.5) RB's. The '24 unit had just two starts lost to injury but dipped to DT HERO KANU POSITION OUTLOOK FOR 2026 QUARTERBACKS - In '24 I called the Quinn Ewers/ Arch Manning combo my #1 rated QB room. Manning added mobility to the unit and got in two starts, throwing for 939 (68%, 9-2), with an affinity for the deep ball and ran for 108 yards. Ewers had a 23-6 ratio but over the last 5 it was 8-6. He threw for 3,472 yards (66%) and left for the NFL (#7 DC). Manning was the preseason Heisman favorite with true frosh KJ Lacey (PS#13) added. Manning had a slow start and even drew early boos from the Texas crowd but finished strong and threw for 3,163 (61.4%, 26-7) with 399 rush. This year they add MJ Morris (PS#19) who has 9 career starts (NCSt, Mary, CCar) and true frosh Dia Bell (PS#3). Manning turned down the NFL and this time is legitimately the Heisman favorite! RUNNING BACKS - In '24 Texas lost their top RB again (#2DC, 1139, 6.1) plus a #5DC (134, 11.2). Tre Wisner led with 1,064 (4.7). Christian Clark had 105 in the bowl and was #2 RB with 234 (4.5). The top 3 RB's had just 1,232 yards and all 3 depart with only Simon back. They add 1st tm ACC Hollywood Smothers (PS#16, 939, 5.9 NCSt) and 1st tm B12 Raleek Brown (PS#4, 1141, 6.1 Ariz St) plus PS#6 and PS#60 true frosh and will easily top '25's pedestrian and injury plagued numbers.
